title: Harness Handbook: Making Evolving Agent Harnesses Readable,Navigable, and Editable
event_hint: arXiv publication on agent harness evolution methodology
problem: Behavior localization is the central bottleneck in harness evolution. Before a modification can be made, developers or coding agents must identify all code locations that implement the target behavior. This is difficult because production harnesses are large, tightly coupled, and behaviorally distributed across files, functions, execution stages, and state transitions, while modification requests describe what the system should do and repositories are organized by files and modules.
mechanism: Harness Handbook: a behavior-centric representation synthesized automatically from a harness codebase through static program analysis and LLM-assisted behavioral structuring, which organizes implementation knowledge around system behaviors and links each behavior to corresponding source code. Also introduces Behavior-Guided Progressive Disclosure (BGPD), which guides coding agents from high-level behavior descriptions to relevant implementation details and verifies candidate locations against current source.

evidence.claim: Harness Handbook organizes implementation knowledge by what the harness does rather than by files and modules, using a three-level hierarchy (L1: system overview, L2: component overview, L3: unit deep dive) with progressive disclosure and behavior-implementation alignment rules.

The construction pipeline uses static analysis to extract program facts (call graph, state accesses, external calls), behavioral organization to map functions to execution stages via a propose-review loop, and hierarchical synthesis to build the L1-L3 handbook.

Abstract claims Handbook-Assisted planning improves behavior localization and edit-plan quality while using fewer planner tokens, with largest gains on scattered implementation sites, rarely executed paths, and cross-module interactions.
evidence.condition: Specific quantitative results, baseline values, and experimental conditions not visible in front evidence pack

evidence.claim: Evaluated on diverse modification requests from two open-source agent harnesses, comparing Baseline vs Handbook-Assisted planning.

evaluation_context: Evaluated on two open-source agent harnesses with diverse modification requests. Comparison is between Baseline planning and Handbook-Assisted BGPD planning on the same tasks. Metrics mentioned include behavior localization, edit-plan quality, and planner token usage. Specific harness names, modification request categories, workload scale, hardware/software deployment details are not visible in front evidence.
limitations: EXPLICIT: None stated in visible evidence. MISSING VALIDATION (front evidence limitation): Quantitative experimental results section not visible in evidence pack; abstract claims improvements without visible baseline values, specific metrics, or statistical validation details. The evidence pack (pages 1-5) contains only abstract, introduction, related work, and representation design sections. No information on index construction overhead, refresh cost, or performance on different harness scales is visible.
project_relevance: DIRECTLY RELEVANT to Agent semantic acceleration (Agent Acceleration topic, Read/Grep direction). The paper addresses behavior localization which is a key part of the 'search symbol-read file-locate call chain-modify-verify' path in coding agents. Behavior-Guided Progressive Disclosure could reduce repeated Read/Grep/tool calls by guiding agents directly to relevant code locations. However, the abstract claims about improved localization and token efficiency lack visible quantitative evidence in the front evidence pack. The approach focuses on behavior-to-code mapping rather than repository indexing acceleration, which is a different angle from traditional code graph/repo graph approaches. The project questions about whether code knowledge graphs reduce end-to-end task latency and whether tool call parallelization introduces correctness risks are partially addressed by this work, but specific evidence on Read/Grep reduction and end-to-end latency is not visible in the front evidence.

Experimental results with specific numbers, baselines, and conditions are in later sections not included in evidence pack.
